summary: Specifies how to carry Fibre Channel traffic over an MPLS network using a pseudowire, so service providers can offer emulated Fibre Channel services over MPLS. It defines the encapsulation and the common procedures for using such a pseudowire.

eli5.summary: Fibre Channel is a way storage systems talk. This wraps those messages in an envelope that can ride across an MPLS network, as if two distant storage boxes were linked by a direct cable.

subtitle: How to carry Fibre Channel storage traffic across an MPLS network so two distant SAN ports behave as if joined by one cable.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel links connect servers to storage in data centers, and sites often need to extend them over long distances. Existing options such as FCIP rely on TCP and need special timing mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: A Fibre Channel pseudowire wraps FC frames, primitive sequences and control frames in an MPLS packet with a 4-octet control word, and trims idle traffic to save bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: The two FC ports act as if directly connected, but the MPLS network must be provisioned with very low loss and low latency because the pseudowire does not repair drops or reordering.

today: RFC 6307 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used together with the Fibre Channel pseudowire portion of the T11 FC-BB-5 Amendment 1 specification.

sections.title: Why Carry Fibre Channel over MPLS
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is a high-speed technology used mainly for Storage Area Networks. When FC is extended across sites, the most common use is storage replication for disaster recovery.

The RFC defines a Fibre Channel pseudowire (FC PW): a method to transparently transport FC traffic over an MPLS network, giving behavior similar to two FC ports joined by a physical FC link. The RFC says this gives simpler control processing than FCIP (RFC 3821), which tunnels FC frames over TCP/IP and needs special timing mechanisms because of delay variation and TCP timeouts.

The complete specification is this document plus the FC PW portion of the T11 standard FC-BB-5/AM1. This RFC covers the encapsulation and the common pseudowire procedures; the FC-specific processing is left to T11.
sections.eli5: Two faraway computers want to share a storage box as if it were in the same room. This RFC explains how to tunnel their messages through a big network so they never notice the distance.

sections.title: Transparency, Efficiency and Reliability Goals
sections.content:
Three requirements shape the design. First, transparency: the PW logically joins the FC port at one end directly to the FC port at the far end, whereas FCIP introduces FC B_Ports at both ends.

Second, bandwidth efficiency. The PW may have less bandwidth than the attached FC port. A native FC link constantly exchanges Idle primitive signals, so the Provider Edge (PE) suppresses them and the far-end PE regenerates them. Repeated primitive sequences are also thinned out: for example, only every fourth primitive may be sent, and the RFC notes that a 10:1 reduction achieves 90% of the bandwidth benefit. The far-end PE keeps sending the most recently received sequence until something new arrives.

Third, reliability. FC has no native frame retransmission, and a lost frame usually fails an I/O operation, with 30-second and 60-second timeouts common before retries. FC also tolerates little reordering. The FC PW does not compensate for drops, discards or reordering; the MPLS network is expected to make them very rare. FC uses a constant delivery timeout (R_A_TOV, default 10 seconds) instead of an IP-style TTL.
sections.eli5: Storage traffic hates losing or shuffling messages, so the network must be very reliable. To save space, the tunnel skips the endless "I'm still here" chatter and the other end makes it up again.

sections.title: Reference Model and Native Service Processing
sections.content:
FC traffic enters at the first PE through its FC attachment channel, is encapsulated, crosses the MPLS network, is decapsulated at the second PE, and leaves through that PE's attachment channel. The pseudowire can be provisioned statically or by a signaling protocol as defined in RFC 4447. The model derives from the PWE3 architecture in RFC 3985.

Inside each PE, Native Service Processing (NSP) does three jobs:

  • Idle Suppression: Idle primitive signals from the local FC port are dropped and regenerated at the far end.
  • Primitive Sequence Reduction: only a subset of repeated primitive sequences is sent over the WAN.
  • Flow Control: the Alternate Simple Flow Control (ASFC) pause/resume protocol manages buffers so traffic is not dropped.

Flow control is needed because FC's credit-based flow control may not have enough buffer credits to fill the bandwidth over the extra distance and latency. The details of NSP are specified in FC-BB-5/AM1.
sections.eli5: Each end has a helper that skips repeating messages, and a pause button to say "slow down, my mailbox is full."

sections.title: Encapsulation and the Control Word
sections.content:
Only three kinds of FC connection are supported: N_Port to N_Port (set up by PLOGI), N_Port to F_Port (FLOGI) and E_Port to E_Port (ELP). Traffic is split into four payload types, carried in the 3-bit PT field: 0 FC data frames, 1 FC login frames, 2 primitive sequences and signals, and 6 FC PW control frames (ASFC flow control, ping, error reports). Packets with any other PT value MUST be discarded.

The generic PW control word from RFC 4385 MUST be used. Its first four bits are zero. The X bit and fragmentation bits SHOULD be zero and are ignored by the receiver. The Length field MUST be used for packets shorter than 64 octets and MUST be zero for longer ones. The sequence number is not used, so it MUST be 0 on send and ignored on receipt.

After the control word comes an FC Encapsulation Header, which this version does not use: it SHOULD be zero and MUST be ignored. The spec is limited to FC service classes 2, 3 and F, and to links using 8b/10b transmission code. Links using 64b/66b (such as 10GFC and 16GFC) MUST NOT be attached unless their speed can be negotiated down to 8b/10b.
sections.eli5: Every tunnel packet starts with a small label saying what is inside: a normal message, a login, a link signal or a tunnel-only note. Anything with an unknown label is thrown away.

sections.title: Mapping Frames, Signals and Control Frames
sections.content:
Data and login frames (PT 0 and 1) share one format: the whole FC frame, including the Start Of Frame delimiter, header, CRC and End Of Frame delimiter, goes in one PW packet. SOF and EOF are each one octet as in RFC 3643, except that delimiters used only by class 4 MUST NOT be used. The CRC is taken from the FC channel and is not recalculated or checked by the PE, so the receiving FC port does the check. This differs from RFC 4720, which requires the FCS to be checked at ingress.

Primitive sequences and signals (PT 2) are FC Ordered Sets: four 10b characters starting with K28.5, then three Dxx.y data characters. The K28.5 is sent as its 8b value 0xBC, which is also the value of D28.5, so the receiver MUST treat the first byte of each Ordered Set as K28.5 and the other three as data characters. A packet may hold several Ordered Sets but MUST NOT exceed 60 octets, so that the Length field is non-zero. The egress PE keeps repeating a received Primitive Sequence until a frame or another Ordered Set arrives; a Primitive Signal is sent once, except Idle, which is sent continuously when nothing else is pending.

Control frames (PT 6) are generated and terminated by the FC entities at the PW ends and are always shorter than 64 octets.

The MTU must fit the largest FC frame after encapsulation. The maximum FC frame is 2164 octets, and the network SHOULD accommodate up to 2500 octets. Fragmentation as in RFC 4623 SHALL NOT be used.
sections.eli5: A whole storage message goes into one envelope, untouched, and the receiver at the far end checks it is not damaged. Short signals can share an envelope, and tunnel-to-tunnel notes always fit in a tiny one.

sections.title: Signaling and Timing
sections.content:
Pseudowires are set up with LDP as in RFC 4447. The PW Type MUST be the new FC Port Mode value. The control word is REQUIRED, so the C-bit MUST be set; otherwise the PW MUST NOT be established and a Label Release with an "Illegal C-Bit" status is sent. The fragmentation indicator, Interface MTU and FCS Retention Indicator parameters MUST be omitted. PW failures MUST be mapped to emulated signal failure indications on the FC link.

Timing is strict. Latency between the two customer edges must be no more than one-half of R_T_TOV (default 100 milliseconds) for primitive sequences, no more than one-half of E_D_TOV (default 2 seconds) for frames, and within R_A_TOV (default 10 seconds) of the fabric. Since R_T_TOV is the smallest, meeting half of it is sufficient. If latency is too high, link initialization may fail, links may drop, or frame identifiers could be reused too early, which could corrupt data.

PE devices SHOULD measure latency with the PING and PING_ACK control frames. If a timing requirement is violated, the PE MUST generate a WAN Down event, which makes it send NOS continuously and halts FC traffic without tearing down the pseudowire itself.
sections.eli5: The tunnel has a strict speed limit on how slow it may be. If messages take too long, the ends say "the line is down" instead of risking mixed-up data.

sections.title: Security and Applicability
sections.content:
Security for the FC PW follows the security sections of RFC 3985 and RFC 4385. FC fabric security protocols (FC-SP) work at higher layers and are transparent to the PW.

The timing rules create an exposure: an attacker who injects enough latency to push round-trip time past R_T_TOV (default 100 ms) can make the PW fail, because link initialization keeps timing out. OAM for deployed FC PWs SHOULD watch for this persisting and respond, for example by shutting the PW down.

On applicability, FC PW traffic should only traverse MPLS networks that are traffic engineered to give dedicated bandwidth, with ingress policing. Otherwise FCIP SHOULD be used instead. The document provides no protection against network outages, so resilience depends on the underlying MPLS network.
sections.eli5: Someone could slow the line on purpose until the tunnel gives up. The advice is to watch for that and use a dedicated, protected network.

fields.name: Zero bits
fields.desc: Set to 0 by the ingress PE to indicate PW data.

fields.name: PT
fields.desc: Payload type: 0 data, 1 login, 2 primitives, 6 PW control.

fields.name: X
fields.desc: Unused; SHOULD be zero and is ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Frag
fields.desc: Bits 8-9; unused, SHOULD be zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Used for packets shorter than 64 octets, zero for longer ones.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Not used; MUST be 0 on send and ignored on receipt.

items.label: FC PW control frame
items.desc: ASFC flow control, ping and error indications between PW endpoints.
